newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan sacks indicted oil monopoly chairman.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan sacks indicted oil monopoly chairman.

text.p: The chairman of Taiwan's state oil monopoly was sacked on Tuesday after being indicted on charges unrelated to his duties at the Chinese Petroleum Corp
Chang Tzu-yuan maintained innocence and accused prosecutors of "putting on a show" by trying to link him to wrongdoings during his earlier tenure as mayor of central Taichung city.
Chang was replaced by Lee Shu-jeou, a vice minister at the Economics Ministry, which oversees the state-owned company, ministry officials said at a news conference.
"Chang Tzu-yuan has been transferred to be an adviser to the ministry," Vice Minister Chang Chang-pang said.
"The reason he is being replaced is that he will face a lot of legal proceedings," Chang said.
Chang Tzu-yuan was charged in connection with land zoning improprieties allegedly committed when he was Taichung mayor from 1985-1989, officials said.
He faces up to six years in prison if convicted.
Chang said he was not surprised by the ministry's decision.
"I will respect (the ministry's) decision, but I promise to fight for the reputation of myself and my family," Chang told reporters after the ministry announced his sacking.
"I am very disturbed by the prosecutor manufacturing a crime for me for the sake of putting on a show," he added.
Chang declined to take questions from reporters.

Chang's indictment was the latest in a string of blows for Taiwan's oil giant. Company president Chen Kuo-young resigned on November 19 to take responsibility for a series of explosions, fires and oil spills that cost the company millions of dollars in compensation claims and fines in 1996.

Chinese Petroleum, which reported a huge budget deficit in November, finally saw its fiscal 1996-97 budget adopted by parliament last Thursday after months of political foot-dragging over its proposed privatisation and other contentious issues.

The budget stalemate and popular opposition have prevented Chinese Petroleum from carrying through oil price increases that would enable it to balance its budget at a time when world oil prices are sharply higher than it had anticipated.

Parliament cut the monopoly's budget for key overseas expansion programmes in Indonesia and Vietnam and cancelled its participation in a consortium planning to build a power station in northern Taiwan.
Before his indictment, Chang had vowed to stay on at Chinese Petroleum despite mounting criticism of his stewardship from lawmakers, government officials and Taiwan's media.
